levels.conclusion: The proved shear-family Green identity applies with coefficient 3 and the stated boundary orientation.

levels.title: Green in flux form
levels.objective: Verify outward planar flux equals the divergence integral.
levels.explanation: For F=(x,y,0), compute outward planar flux using the four specified unit conormals, then compute the integral of divergence 2. Right and top edges contribute 1 each; bottom and left contribute zero. Equality of these independent calculations verifies the flux-form Green special case, with outward conormals distinct from boundary tangent directions.
levels.statement: : squareOutwardFlux (fun p => ![p 0,p 1,0]) = (∫ x : ℝ in 0..1, ∫ y : ℝ in 0..1, divergence (fun p => ![p 0,p 1,0]) ![x,y,0])
levels.proof:
have boundary : squareOutwardFlux (fun p => ![p 0,p 1,0]) = 2 := by
  rw [squareOutwardFlux]
  norm_num [dot]
have insideValue : (∫ x : ℝ in 0..1, ∫ y : ℝ in 0..1, divergence (fun p => ![p 0,p 1,0]) ![x,y,0]) = 2 := by
  norm_num [divergence, partial_coordinate, partial_constant]
rw [boundary, insideValue]
hints: Evaluate the outward edge sum as one named boundary value.
Compute matching-coordinate derivatives for the interior value.
Rewrite both sides using those independent calculations.
levels.conclusion: Independent outward-flux and divergence calculations verify this flux-form Green special case.

levels.title: Boss: area from the boundary
levels.objective: Recover enclosed area from a boundary circulation.
levels.explanation: The area formula uses the boundary field (-y/2,x/2,0), whose planar curl is 1. Compute the boundary integral directly on the four positively oriented edges, then compare with the double integral of 1. The two nonzero edge contributions are each 1/2. This proves the stated area identity for the unit square.
levels.statement: : squareCirculation rotation = (∫ x : ℝ in 0..1, ∫ y : ℝ in 0..1, (1:ℝ)) ∧ squareCirculation rotation = 1
levels.proof:
have circulation : squareCirculation rotation = 1 := by
  have edge1 : work (rotation) (fun t => ![t,0,0]) 0 1 = 0 := by
    norm_num [work, dot, velocity_components, deriv_const_sub_id, rotation]
  have edge2 : work (rotation) (fun t => ![1,t,0]) 0 1 = 1/2 := by
    norm_num [work, dot, velocity_components, deriv_const_sub_id, rotation]
  have edge3 : work (rotation) (fun t => ![1-t,1,0]) 0 1 = 1/2 := by
    norm_num [work, dot, velocity_components, deriv_const_sub_id, rotation]
  have edge4 : work (rotation) (fun t => ![0,1-t,0]) 0 1 = 0 := by
    norm_num [work, dot, velocity_components, deriv_const_sub_id, rotation]
  rw [squareCirculation, edge1, edge2, edge3, edge4]
  norm_num
constructor
· rw [circulation]
  norm_num [constant_integral]
· exact circulation
hints: Use the rotational field and the positive square boundary.
Compute and add its four work integrals.
Compare the resulting circulation with the integral of the constant area density.
levels.conclusion: The rotational boundary integral equals the square’s area 1.

title: Surface Expedition
prerequisites: Cross products; partial derivatives; double integration.

levels.title: Parametrize a surface
levels.objective: Verify that a patch lies in a specified surface.
levels.explanation:
A surface parametrization has two independent parameters. `patch u v` maps (u,v) to (u,v,0), placing every point in the horizontal plane. Read its height and two planar coordinates directly. The parameter rectangle used later fixes the actual bounded patch.

Worked example: For s(u,v)=(u,v,u+v), substituting (1,2) gives (1,2,3). A surface uses two parameter inputs.
levels.statement: (u v : ℝ) : (patch u v) 2 = 0 ∧ (patch u v) 0 = u ∧ (patch u v) 1 = v
levels.proof:
constructor
· rfl
· constructor
  · rfl
  · rfl
hints: Separate the height and the two planar coordinates.
Read the explicit formula for `patch`.
Each coordinate identity follows by `rfl`.
levels.conclusion: The two-parameter map lies in the horizontal plane and retains its planar coordinates.

levels.title: Tangents and normal
levels.objective: Compute the two parameter tangents and their oriented cross product.
levels.explanation:
Differentiate the surface while holding v fixed, then while holding u fixed. These are the two tangent vectors. Their cross product in the stated order is the oriented normal, including the area factor. Name both tangent calculations and reuse them in `surfaceNormal`.

Worked example: For s(u,v)=(2u,v,0), parameter tangents are (2,0,0) and (0,1,0), so the oriented area vector is (0,0,2).
levels.statement: (u v : ℝ) : velocity (fun t => patch t v) u = (![1,0,0] : Vec) ∧ velocity (patch u) v = (![0,1,0] : Vec) ∧ surfaceNormal patch u v = (![0,0,1] : Vec)
levels.proof:
have du : velocity (fun t => patch t v) u = (![1,0,0] : Vec) := by
  simp only [patch, velocity_components]
  apply vector_eq
  · norm_num
  · norm_num
  · norm_num
have dv : velocity (patch u) v = (![0,1,0] : Vec) := by
  have coordinates (t : ℝ) : patch u t = (![u,t,0] : Vec) := by rfl
  rw [velocity_congr coordinates, velocity_components]
  apply vector_eq
  · norm_num
  · norm_num
  · norm_num
constructor
· exact du
· constructor
  · exact dv
  · rw [surfaceNormal, du, dv]
    apply vector_eq
    · norm_num [cross]
    · norm_num [cross]
    · norm_num [cross]
hints: Name the derivative in each parameter direction.
Use `velocity_components` for each scalar component.
Rewrite `surfaceNormal` with the two tangent values and calculate their cross product.
levels.conclusion: The parameter tangents give the upward oriented normal (0,0,1).

levels.title: Area factor
levels.objective: Compute the Euclidean surface-area density.
levels.explanation: The surface-area factor is the Euclidean length of the parameter normal. The general rule `normal_components` computes that normal from the two parameter derivatives. For this patch its value is (0,0,1), so its length is 1. Scalar area uses the length, while flux retains the orientation vector. A named coordinate formula is passed to `normal_congr` to replace the surface before computing its derivative columns.
levels.statement: (u v : ℝ) : length (surfaceNormal patch u v) = 1
levels.proof:
have normal (s t : ℝ) : surfaceNormal patch s t = (![0,0,1] : Vec) := by
  have coordinates (a b : ℝ) : patch a b = (![a,b,0] : Vec) := by rfl
  rw [normal_congr coordinates, normal_components]
  apply vector_eq
  · norm_num [partialX, partialY, cross]
  · norm_num [partialX, partialY, cross]
  · norm_num [partialX, partialY, cross]
rw [normal]
norm_num [length, lengthSq, dot]
hints: Compute the normal from the two parameter derivative columns.
Substitute the normal into the length.
Evaluate its squared Euclidean length and square root.
levels.conclusion: The parameter normal has Euclidean length 1, the required scalar area factor.

levels.title: A scalar surface integral
levels.objective: Integrate a scalar density with the area factor.
levels.explanation: A scalar surface integral multiplies the scalar density at the surface point by the area factor. Here the density is u and the factor is 1. Name the normal, evaluate the inner integral as u, and integrate it over [0,1]. The increasing parameter bounds give nonnegative area weighting.
levels.proof:
have normal (s t : ℝ) : surfaceNormal patch s t = (![0,0,1] : Vec) := by
  have coordinates (a b : ℝ) : patch a b = (![a,b,0] : Vec) := by rfl
  rw [normal_congr coordinates, normal_components]
  apply vector_eq
  · norm_num [partialX, partialY, cross]
  · norm_num [partialX, partialY, cross]
  · norm_num [partialX, partialY, cross]
have innerValue (u : ℝ) : (∫ v : ℝ in 0..1, (fun p : Vec => p 0) (patch u v) * length (surfaceNormal patch u v)) = u := by
  norm_num [normal, patch, length, lengthSq, dot, constant_integral]
rw [surfaceIntegral, integral_values innerValue, integral_id]
norm_num
hints: Calculate the parameter normal and hence its length.
Prove the inner scalar integral equals u.
Replace it under the outer integral and integrate u.
levels.conclusion: The scalar surface integral of the first coordinate equals 1/2.

levels.title: Oriented flux
levels.objective: Integrate a vector field against an oriented area vector.
levels.explanation: Flux of the upward unit field through this upward-oriented patch uses the dot product with the unnormalized parameter normal. Its integrand is 1. Calculate that oriented integrand before integrating; no additional area-factor multiplication is needed.
levels.proof:
have normal (s t : ℝ) : surfaceNormal patch s t = (![0,0,1] : Vec) := by
  have coordinates (a b : ℝ) : patch a b = (![a,b,0] : Vec) := by rfl
  rw [normal_congr coordinates, normal_components]
  apply vector_eq
  · norm_num [partialX, partialY, cross]
  · norm_num [partialX, partialY, cross]
  · norm_num [partialX, partialY, cross]
have innerValue (u : ℝ) : (∫ v : ℝ in 0..1, dot (![0,0,1] : Vec) (surfaceNormal patch u v)) = 1 := by
  norm_num [normal, dot, constant_integral]
rw [surfaceFlux, integral_values innerValue, constant_integral]
norm_num
hints: Reuse the upward parameter normal.
Calculate the inner integral of the field-normal dot product.
Replace it and evaluate the outer constant integral.
levels.conclusion: The upward unit field has flux 1 through the upward patch.

levels.title: Boss: reverse the patch
levels.objective: Compare equal scalar area and opposite oriented flux.
levels.explanation: Interchanging the parameter order reverses the normal while preserving its length. Calculate both normals, the two fluxes, and the two scalar areas. Then compare the results. This distinguishes orientation-sensitive flux from orientation-independent area by a fully checked concrete example.
levels.statement: : surfaceFlux (fun _ => ![0,0,1]) (fun u v => ![v,u,0]) 0 1 0 1 = -surfaceFlux (fun _ => ![0,0,1]) patch 0 1 0 1 ∧ surfaceIntegral (fun _ => 1) (fun u v => ![v,u,0]) 0 1 0 1 = surfaceIntegral (fun _ => 1) patch 0 1 0 1
levels.proof:
have normal (s t : ℝ) : surfaceNormal patch s t = (![0,0,1] : Vec) := by
  have coordinates (a b : ℝ) : patch a b = (![a,b,0] : Vec) := by rfl
  rw [normal_congr coordinates, normal_components]
  apply vector_eq
  · norm_num [partialX, partialY, cross]
  · norm_num [partialX, partialY, cross]
  · norm_num [partialX, partialY, cross]
have reversed (u v : ℝ) : surfaceNormal (fun s t => ![t,s,0]) u v = (![0,0,-1] : Vec) := by
  rw [normal_components]
  apply vector_eq
  · norm_num [partialX, partialY, cross]
  · norm_num [partialX, partialY, cross]
  · norm_num [partialX, partialY, cross]
have upFlux : surfaceFlux (fun _ => ![0,0,1]) patch 0 1 0 1 = 1 := by
  norm_num [surfaceFlux, normal, dot]
have downFlux : surfaceFlux (fun _ => ![0,0,1]) (fun u v => ![v,u,0]) 0 1 0 1 = -1 := by
  norm_num [surfaceFlux, reversed, dot]
have upArea : surfaceIntegral (fun _ => 1) patch 0 1 0 1 = 1 := by
  norm_num [surfaceIntegral, normal, length, lengthSq, dot]
have downArea : surfaceIntegral (fun _ => 1) (fun u v => ![v,u,0]) 0 1 0 1 = 1 := by
  norm_num [surfaceIntegral, reversed, length, lengthSq, dot]
constructor
· rw [downFlux, upFlux]
· rw [downArea, upArea]
hints: Calculate the original and reversed parameter normals.
Use those normals to name the two fluxes and the two areas.
Substitute the four values into the requested comparisons.
levels.conclusion: Parameter reversal negates flux while preserving scalar surface area.

title: Stokes Summit
prerequisites: Curl; positively oriented boundaries; parametrized surface flux.

The four sides of the parameter square give the patch boundary. Traverse them with u increasing on the bottom, v increasing on the right, u decreasing on the top, and v decreasing on the left. Verify all four traces; these are the oriented edge curves used in the square circulation.

Worked example: For a stretched rectangle s(u,v)=(2u,v,0), fixing v=0 gives its bottom edge (2u,0,0). Fix a parameter to obtain each edge.

constructor
· rfl
· constructor
  · rfl
  · constructor
    · rfl
    · rfl

Keep decreasing parameters on the top and left.
Separate the four trace equalities and read their coordinates.
levels.conclusion: All four parameter-edge restrictions give the stated oriented boundary traces.

levels.title: Match orientations
levels.objective: Verify the normal and oriented top boundary agree.
levels.explanation:
The upward parameter normal matches a counterclockwise boundary by the right-hand rule. Along the top edge, the tangent must point in the negative x direction. Verify both the surface normal and this oriented boundary tangent; matching a set of boundary points alone would not determine orientation.

Worked example: A downward normal matches clockwise boundary motion when viewed from above. Reversing both orientations preserves the Stokes sign relation.

levels.proof:
have normal (s t : ℝ) : surfaceNormal patch s t = (![0,0,1] : Vec) := by
  have coordinates (a b : ℝ) : patch a b = (![a,b,0] : Vec) := by rfl
  rw [normal_congr coordinates, normal_components]
  apply vector_eq
  · norm_num [partialX, partialY, cross]
  · norm_num [partialX, partialY, cross]
  · norm_num [partialX, partialY, cross]
constructor
· exact normal 0 0
· simp only [patch, velocity_components]
  apply vector_eq
  · norm_num [deriv_const_sub_id]
  · norm_num [deriv_const_sub_id]
  · norm_num [deriv_const_sub_id]
hints: Calculate the upward surface normal.
Differentiate the top-edge parametrization with its decreasing first coordinate.
Check that its tangent is (-1,0,0).
levels.conclusion: The upward normal matches the negative-x tangent on the top boundary edge.

levels.title: Curl through a patch
levels.objective: Compute the curl flux integrand in Stokes’ formula.
levels.explanation: Stokes uses curl F dotted with the parameter normal. Compute the normal and the cross-coordinate derivatives for F=(0,x,0). Its curl points upward, so the dot product is 1. Keeping the normal vector rather than only its length preserves the orientation sign.

norm_num [partial_coordinate, partial_constant]

Open the curl formula and use the coordinate partial rules.
Take the oriented dot product.

levels.title: The boundary calculation
levels.objective: Evaluate circulation with the orientation induced by the surface.
levels.explanation: Evaluate boundary circulation directly for F=(0,2x,0). Use the same four oriented edges as in Green’s Garden. Only the upward right edge contributes, with value 2. This independently checks the boundary side before invoking the surface theorem.

have edge1 : work (fun p => ![0,2*p 0,0]) (fun t => ![t,0,0]) 0 1 = 0 := by
  norm_num [work, dot, velocity_components, deriv_const_sub_id]
have edge2 : work (fun p => ![0,2*p 0,0]) (fun t => ![1,t,0]) 0 1 = 2 := by
  norm_num [work, dot, velocity_components, deriv_const_sub_id]
have edge3 : work (fun p => ![0,2*p 0,0]) (fun t => ![1-t,1,0]) 0 1 = 0 := by

norm_num

Retain the top and left reversal signs in their velocities.
Add the four named values using `squareCirculation`.

levels.title: Apply Stokes: square patch
levels.objective: Apply an established Stokes special-case family.

hints: Recognize coefficient 2 in the shear field.
Check that the boundary and patch orientations match the proved family.
Apply `stokes_shear_patch`.

The graph-normal rule `normal_graph` has vertical component 1, and this field has vertical unit curl, so both flux integrands equal 1. Together with the proved flat-patch Stokes family, this justifies the simpler-surface calculation in this concrete case; it does not assume a general surface-independence theorem.

        · norm_num [liftedPatch, patch]

Use `normal_graph` to identify the vertical area-vector component.
Evaluate both curl fluxes and compare their values.

title: Gauss Citadel
prerequisites: Divergence; oriented surface flux; triple integrals; integral theorem special cases.

levels.objective: Verify outward orientation on all six cube faces.
levels.explanation:
A closed cube has six faces, and every face must point outward. The parameter order differs between opposite faces. Calculate all six cross-product normals: +x, -x, +y, -y, +z, -z. The same six parametrizations occur in `cubeFlux`, so the closed-boundary orientation is fully explicit.

Use `normal_components` for each parametrization.

levels.title: Divergence in the solid
levels.objective: Integrate a field divergence over the cube.
levels.explanation:
For the smooth radial field, the three matching coordinate partials give divergence 3. Establish that formula at an arbitrary point before evaluating its triple integral. The unit cube has unit volume, so integrating this constant gives 3. This is the volume side of the divergence identity.

Worked example: For F=(2x,2y,2z), divergence is 6. On a unit cube its volume integral is 6 times volume 1.

levels.proof:

  rw [divergence]
  norm_num [radial, partial_coordinate]
norm_num [div, constant_integral]
hints: Name the divergence formula for an arbitrary point.
Compute its three matching-coordinate partials.
Integrate the resulting constant over the unit cube.
levels.conclusion: The unit-cube divergence volume integral equals 3.

levels.objective: Compute flux directly on the six outward-oriented faces.

Name the six actual surface integrals before adding them in `cubeFlux`. This calculation does not use the divergence theorem.

norm_num

Use the face normals to distinguish positive and zero contributions.
Rewrite the six-face sum with those values and add.

levels.title: Apply Gauss on a cube
levels.objective: Apply a proved divergence-theorem family with verified orientation.
levels.explanation: Apply the proved divergence-theorem family for F=(ax,by,cz) on the outward unit cube. The specified field has coefficients 2, 3, and 4. Smoothness, the bounded solid, and six face orientations are built into this verified special case. The theorem does not assert a result for arbitrary closed surfaces.

hints: Recognize the diagonal linear field.
Identify coefficients 2, 3, and 4 and the outward cube boundary.
Apply `gauss_diagonal`.

levels.title: Recover a missing face
levels.objective: Deduce an unknown flux from the closed-boundary total.
levels.explanation: The five known outward face fluxes sum to 5. Find the missing top flux by first using the unit-cube Gauss theorem to calculate total flux. The general matching-partial rule `divergence_diagonal` gives divergence 2+3+4=9. Rewrite the balance equation and solve the remaining linear equation. The balance assumption states the geometric decomposition, not the requested missing value.

have total : cubeFlux (fun p => ![2*p 0,3*p 1,4*p 2]) = 9 := by
  rw [gauss_diagonal]
  norm_num [divergence_diagonal]
rw [total] at h
linarith
hints: Use `gauss_diagonal` to replace total flux with a volume integral.
Evaluate the constant divergence using `divergence_diagonal`.
Substitute the total in the face balance and solve with `linarith`.
levels.conclusion: Gauss gives total flux 9; subtracting the known contribution 5 gives missing flux 4.

levels.title: Final boss: three integral bridges
levels.objective: Combine justified special cases of Green, Stokes, and Gauss.
levels.explanation: Combine three established integral bridges. Use the shear Green and Stokes identities on the positive square and upward patch. Use the diagonal Gauss family on the outward cube, noting that coefficients (1,1,1) reconstruct the radial field. Evaluate circulation 2 and flux 3 through their interior integrals, then add them. All three applications are justified proved special cases; the final boss introduces no new tactic.
levels.statement: : (squareCirculation (fun p => ![0,2*p 0,0]) = ∫ x : ℝ in 0..1, ∫ y : ℝ in 0..1, (curl (fun p => ![0,2*p 0,0]) ![x,y,0]) 2) ∧ (squareCirculation (fun p => ![0,2*p 0,0]) = surfaceFlux (curl (fun p => ![0,2*p 0,0])) patch 0 1 0 1) ∧ (cubeFlux radial = ∫ x : ℝ in 0..1, ∫ y : ℝ in 0..1, ∫ z : ℝ in 0..1, divergence radial ![x,y,z]) ∧ squareCirculation (fun p => ![0,2*p 0,0]) + cubeFlux radial = 5
levels.proof:
have gauss : cubeFlux radial = ∫ x : ℝ in 0..1, ∫ y : ℝ in 0..1, ∫ z : ℝ in 0..1, divergence radial ![x,y,z] := by
  have rule := gauss_diagonal 1 1 1
  simp only [one_mul, vector_components] at rule
  exact rule
constructor
· apply green_shear
· constructor
  · apply stokes_shear_patch
  · constructor
    · exact gauss
    · have circulation : squareCirculation (fun p => ![0,2*p 0,0]) = 2 := by
        rw [green_shear]
        norm_num [curl, partial_scaled_coordinate, partial_constant]
      have flux : cubeFlux radial = 3 := by
        rw [gauss]
        norm_num [divergence, radial, partial_coordinate]
      rw [circulation, flux]
      norm_num
hints: Identify the Green, Stokes, and Gauss families and their orientations.
For Gauss, instantiate coefficients 1,1,1 and use `vector_components` to reconstruct the radial field.
Evaluate the two interior integrals, then combine their values.
levels.conclusion: The verified Green, Stokes, and Gauss bridges give circulation 2 and flux 3, with combined value 5.
